Settlement of River Water Disputes 
†*164.   DR. D. MASTHAN: 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Commission for Integrated Water Resources 
Development has expressed its opinion that the existing law is inadequate to 
settle the river water disputes; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; 
(c) whether it is a fact that several d isputes regarding sharing of river 
waters are pending; if so, what are these disputes together with the names of 
the States where these disputes exist; and 
(d) the steps Government propose to take to settje these disputes? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (DR. C.P. THAKUR): (a) to 
(d) In order to ensure that awards of inter -state water tribunals are given 
within a reasonable period of time as also the effectiveness of such awards, 
National Commission for Integrated Water Resources Development Plan has 
recommended to amend the Inter State Water Disputes Act, 1956. An 
Implementation Cell in the National Water Development Agency has been 
constituted to examine recommendations' of the National Commission and 
suggest to Union Government about the implementability or o ther-wise of the 
recommendations and to suggest modalities for impementation of such 
recommendations, as found implementable. An Advisory Committee under 
the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Water Commission has been 
constituted for assisting the implemen tation cell in examining the 
recommendations. 
The Inter -State Water Disputes viz. Ravi -Beas Water Dispute between 
Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan and the Cauvery Water Disputes between 
Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and the Union Territory of Pondicherry were  
referred to the Tribunals under the provisions of the Inter State Water Dispute 
Act, 1956 (ISWD Act, 1956) for adjudication in April, 1986 and June, 1990 
respectively. Ravi-Beas Waters Tribunal has submitted its fact finding report 
on 30.1.1987. Party Sta tes and the Central Government have sought 
explanation/guidance under Section 5(3) of ISWD Act, 1956. The Cauvery 
Water Disputes Tribunal has passed an interim order on June 25, 1991.

(d) India receives a rainfall of about 4000 billion cu.m. every year. Out of this

Development for which technical and financial assistance is provided to the 
State Government and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water 
Board has also taken up pilot stu dies for artificial ground water recharge. The 
rooftop rain water harvestiang structures are quite large in number and are 
mostly at individual level and, therefore it is difficult to assess their storage 
capacity. Its contribution towards storage can only  be marginal in comparison 
to the storage through conventional methods.

tried a couple of times to engage the hijackers in a dialogue. But the hijackers

the bowser close to the aircraft, it took off without ATC clearance. When the 
aircraft landed at Amritsar, concrete and specific information in respect of the 
numbers, nationality, weaponry, professionalism and com mitment of the 
hijackers was scantly and speculative. On the other hand, messages being 
received from the hijacked aircraft were tense and demanding. Precipitate 
action, in the absence of even basic information was judged as being fraught 
with unacceptable levels of risk. 
(b) and (c) On the occurence of the hijacking, institutional mechanisms to 
deal with situation were immediately put into action. The Crisis Management 
Group (CMG) and the Central Committee met to address the evolving 
situation. The NSG Tas k Force was also placed on full alert. On the basis of 
available facts, the CMG came to conclusion that the aircraft could not go 
anywhere unless refuelled. The CMG and others concerned acted in the best 
possible way under the given situation.

The Report brings out that the high rate of growth in the nominal stock of 
debt has translated itself into a n accelerated growth of interest payments, 
putting pressure on resource base of the States. The Report brings out that the 
State would have to make efforts to contain non -plan revenue expenditure and 
augment revenue through broadening tax base and cost recovery. 
State Governments are autonomous under the Constitution and take 
measures of their preference from time to time for improving their financial 
condition. Review of the finances of the Union and the States and suggesting 
ways and means by which the Go vernments collectively and severally may 
bring about a restructuring of the public finances so as to restore budgetary 
balance and maintain macroeconomic stability, is also within the terms of 
reference of the Eleventh Finance Commission which is currently in office.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) Under the 
Constitution of India, there is a single integrated system of Courts for the 
Union as well as the States which administer both Union and State laws, and 
at the head of the entire system stands the Supreme Court of India. Below the 
Supreme Court of India stand the High Courts of the different States and under 
each High Court there is a hierarchy of other courts called subordinate courts.

shall have superintendence over all court s and tribunals throughout the 
territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction. The said article further 
provides that the High Court may call for returns from such courts; make and 
issue general rules and prescribe forms for regulating the practice and 
proceedings of such courts; and prescribe forms in which books, entries and 
accounts shall be kept by the officers of any such courts.

Cleaning of the Ganga 
1349. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Mi nister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state. 
(a) whether a major project for cleaning the Ganga was launched during 
the Prime Ministership of late Shri Rajiv Gandhi; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the results achieved so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE  MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. Ganga Action Plan, Phase -I was launched during the Prime Ministership 
of Shri Rajeev Gandhi in June, 1985. 261 schemes of pollution abatement of 
various categories such as int erception, diversion and treatment of municipal 
wastewater, installation of crematoria, river front development works and low 
cost sanitation etc. were sanctioned at a cost of Rs. 462.04 crore in 25 class -
"I" towns in the three States of Uttar Pradesh, Bih ar and West Bengal. 258 
schemes have since been completed which include 32 sewage treatment 
plants. The total expenditure incurred so far is Rs. 451.70 crore under this 
programme. With this, out of the 873 million litres per day of domestic waste 
water targeted 
1 67 

RAJYA SABHA                    [7 March, 2000] 
for interception, diversion and treatment, a capacity to treat 835 million litres 
per day of wastewater has been created. With the completion of these 
schemes, it has been possible to minimise the organic pollution reaching the 
river Ganga. Water quality of river has shown improvement wherever 
completed works are functional. However, there has been only an incidental 
reduction in the level of microbial pollution of the treated sewage reaching the 
river. 
Ganga Action Plan, Phase —"II" has been approved in stages by the 
Government of India between April, 1993 to October, 1996.About 1861 
million litres per day of domestic wastewater is targeted for interception, 
diversion and treatment under this phase.  The total sanctioned cost is Rs. 
1276.26 crore and this includes the following schemes for implementation in 
95 towns in 5 States. 
1. Interception and diversion 
2. Sewage treatment plant 
3. Electric and wood-based crematoria 
4. Low cost sanitation 
5. River front development works. 
Mingling for North-South rivers 
†1350. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
 SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided for considering the possibilities to 
mingle the rivers flowing in the North and South India; 
(b) if so, the action taken by Government in this regard; and 
(c) the names of the rivers of the country identified for mingling? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) The 
erstwhile Ministry of Irrigation (now Ministry of Water Resources) and 
Central Water Commission had in 1980 formulated a National Perspective 
Plan for Water Resources Development which envisages inter linkages 
between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water 
from surplus basins to water deficit basins for optimum utilisation of water 
resources. The Peninsular rivers are Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, 
Cauvery, Vaigai, 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
168 

[7 March, 2000]                      RAJYA SABHA 
Parbati, Kalisindh, Chambal, Damanganga, Pinjal, Par, Tapi, Narmada, Ken, 
Betwa, Pamba, Achankovil, Bedti, Varda, Netravati and Hemavati. The 
Himalayan Rivers are Kosi, Mechi, Ghagra, Gandak, Ganga,  Yamuna, Sarda, 
Sabarmati, Sone, Brahmaputra, Domadar and Subernarekha. The Government 
of India has established National Water Development Agency (NWDA) as an 
Autonomous Society in July, 1982 to carry out the water balance and other 
studies of National Per spective Plan and to prepare feasibility report of the 
links. NWDA has completed prefeasibility report of 31 water transfer links 
and feasibility report of 5 water transfer links. Implementation of Water 
transfer link proposal depends on how soon the detai led project report are 
prepared, consensus       is reached among the concerned States and 
availability of funds.

including replenishable Groundwater is being used for various purposes such

for irrigation and drinking purposes is about 88%. 
(b) As per Land Use Statistics brought out by Ministry of Agriculture for 
the year 1996-97 (latest), the Net Sown Area in the country is 1 42.82 Million

constituting 38.61%.

Subarnarekha Dam Project 
1355. DR. M.N. DAS: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of years which have elapsed since the Subarnarekha River 
Dam Project was cleared by Government and the reasons for inordinate delay 
in implementing it; 
(b) whether there is any possibility of its construction in the near future; 
and 
(c) if not, the reasons for the delay? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) There is 
no project named "Subarnarekha River Dam Project." However, Subarnarekha 
Multi-purpose Project of Bihar, Subarnarekha Barrage Project of West Bengal 
and Subarnarekha Irrigation Project of Orissa have been considered by the 
Union Government for their clearance. The Subarnarekha Multi -purpose 
Project of Bihar was accepted by the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) 
on irrigation, flood control and multi-purpose projects in 1982 for an estimated 
cost of Rs. 480.90 crore. The project co^t was up- dated to Rs. 1428.82 crore 
(1990 price level) and the same was accepted by the TAC in 1992 subject to 
environment and forests clearance from Ministry of Environment & Forests, 
clearance of R&R plans fro m Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, 
and concurrence of State Finance Department. Environment clearance from 
Ministry of Environment & Forests, clearance of R&R plan from Ministry of 
Social Justice and Empowerment and concurrence of State Finance 
Department have been obtained. The forest clearance from Ministry of 
Environment & Forests has not yet been obtained by the Government of Bihar. 
The Subarnarekha Barrage Project of West Bengal and Subarnarekha 
Irrigation Project of Orissa were cleared in 1 995. Though the work in Bihar 
and Orissa portion is yet to be started by the respective State Governments, the 
work in the West Bengal portion is yet to be started by the West Bengal State 
Government. Water being a State subject, execution and completion o f the 
irrigation projects depend upon the priority attached to it by the respective 
State Governments.

Generation of Irrigation Capacity 
† 1358. DR. D.MASTHAN: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have made an estimate of the 
requirement of irrigation in the country; 
(b) if so, to what extent irrigation capacity is required to be generated; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that a time bound plan has been prepared to 
meet this requirement; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Net 
Sown Area in the country is 142.82 million hectares as per Land Use Statistics 
brought out by the Mi nistry of Agriculture for the year 1996 -97 (latest). 
Against this, Ultimate Irrigation Potential (UIP) in the country has been 
assessed as 139.89 million hecatres (m.ha.) Out of this, irrigation capacity of 
89.56 m.ha has already been created by the end of  the Eighth Five Year Plan, 
leaving 50.33 m.ha. of irrigajion capacity to be generated. 
(c) and (d) Creation of irrigation capacity is a continuous process and for 
this purpose the State Governments take up major, medium, and minor 
irrigation projects. In the Ninth Five Year Plan, target of creating additional 
irrigation capacity of 17.05 m.ha. comprising 9.81 m.ha. from major and 
medium irrigation projects and 7.24 m.ha. from minor irrigation schemes, has 
been set. Outlays of Rs. 42644 crore for major and medium irrigation sector 
and Rs. 8985 crore for minor irrigation sector have been provided in the Ninth 
Plan (State Sector) for development of irrigation facilities in the country. 
Besides plan allocation, the Union Government is also providing Central Loa n 
Assistance to the States through Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme 
for expeditious completion of on -going major & medium irrigation projects, 
which are languishing for want of funds. Also the Government of India has 
prepared a National Perspectiv e Plan for transfer of water from surplus areas 
to water deficit areas. As per preliminary assessment, it is envisaged that 
additional irrigation capacity of 35 million hectares would be feasible through 
inter-basin transfer of water.
